# Muskan Paliwal — Entire CLI contribution study guide

Research snapshot: **8 September 2026**. Identity: Git author **Muskan Paliwal**, GitHub **MuskanPaliwal**. Scope: `entireio/cli`, this clone's reachable history, and live GitHub PR metadata.

## What I found, and how to read this

I found **32 PRs authored by your account: 12 merged, 18 open, and 2 closed without merging**. One of those closed PRs, **#1996**, was incorporated into **#1877**, which was authored by another contributor and merged. That is delivered work worth discussing; it would disappear from an inventory restricted to your merged PRs.

The frozen local Git inventory contains **390 authored objects: 111 non-merge source/documentation commits, 112 merge or merge-shaped stash objects, and 167 checkpoint/snapshot/stash objects**. These are object counts, not feature counts. Rebased copies, follow-up fixes, integration merges, and Entire's own captured snapshots inflate them. The companion [commit inventory](MUSKAN-COMMIT-INVENTORY.md) identifies every object in this snapshot and associates implementation commits with their contribution families.

Your earliest source commit here is **11 May 2026**, followed by work in May and June and a much denser run in August–September. I did not impose a one-month cutoff and accidentally omit the earlier work.

**Evidence method.** I inspected author history across local refs, PR author/state/head/merge metadata, changed-file diffs, implementations and callers at the relevant historical revision, and regression-test code. I used Entire navigation and selected checkpoint transcripts to recover context. For merged PRs, the account below uses the **merge result**, rather than an intermediate branch that may have changed later. For open PRs, it uses the **observed PR head**. Two unavailable local heads were inspected through GitHub's diff. Links below pin source to these revisions. Tests described here are inspected coverage, **not a claim that I reran those suites**.

**Completeness boundary.** This covers the authored PRs returned by GitHub for this repository and commits reachable in the available clone. It cannot enumerate deleted, unfetched, or unreachable historical objects. The workspace checkout is older than several merged contributions, so looking only at today's files in the working directory would produce an inaccurate account. The metadata inventory is frozen because Entire can create additional checkpoint objects while a session runs.

**Credit boundary.** Authorship is evidence of a contribution, not exclusive ownership of every line in a PR. #2038 includes substantial collaborator fixes and tests; #1996 was folded into another author's larger attach feature. I call those boundaries out explicitly.

{{inventory}}

## The architecture your contributions sit inside

A useful starting picture is:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Agent hooks and transcript formats] --> B[Agent adapters: normalize lifecycle events]
    B --> C[Lifecycle dispatch and durable session state]
    C --> D[Manual-commit strategy]
    D --> E[Ephemeral shadow checkpoints]
    D --> F[Condensation into persistent checkpoints]
    G[Git commit hooks and checkpoint trailers] --> D
    F --> H[Checkpoint write requests and backend routing]
    H --> I[Git branch storage]
    H --> J[Per-checkpoint Git refs]
    I --> K[Push queue and pre-push redaction / OPF]
    J --> K
    L[Git metadata resolver and rooted filesystem handles] --> C
    L --> E
    L --> H
    M[Native Git ref transactions] --> E
    M --> I
    M --> J
```

A **session** is the continuing agent interaction. A **turn** is a prompt/response cycle within it. A **checkpoint** packages captured context; an ephemeral checkpoint supports work in progress, while a persistent checkpoint is suitable for later retrieval and syncing. **Condensation** turns the current captured window into persistent checkpoint data and advances session bookkeeping. A user commit can link to that checkpoint through an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.

Three different identities repeatedly matter in your work:

- **Worktree identity:** a checkout has its own administrative Git directory and HEAD, while several worktrees share objects, refs, and Entire state through the common Git directory.
- **Checkpoint identity:** an ID is reserved and later published; the ID format and existing migrated copies influence which backend owns a retry.
- **Filesystem identity:** two differently spelled paths can name the same directory or lock inode. String equality cannot always establish ownership or lock ordering.

Similarly, three different guarantees should stay separate: a file rename publishes one file; a Git ref transaction publishes one or several refs; a durable session-state update records progress for recovery. None automatically makes the entire lifecycle one transaction.

## Contribution dossiers

The entries below cover the requested problem, previous architecture, actual change and call path, important symbols, design decisions, architectural fit, concepts, questions, and details to remember. Larger changes receive more space; related split PRs cross-reference their common architecture without counting it twice.

{{pr:2211}}

**Problem and previous architecture.** The pre-push OPF path builds rewritten checkpoint history with the required redaction/filtering applied. It then has to publish the new tip without discarding a concurrent writer's checkpoint. A go-git reference check/update was insufficient as the interoperability boundary with native Git clients. Imagine OPF reading tip **A**, a hook publishing **B**, and OPF attempting to replace the ref with rewritten **A′**. Blind publication loses B; blindly treating B as covered by the earlier rewrite is also wrong.

**What you changed and the call path.** `RewriteQueuedCheckpointRefsWithOPF` now reaches `checkpoint.CASPersistentRef`, which delegates publication to `gitrepo.CompareAndSwapRef`. The V1 branch path, `RewriteUnpushedV1WithOPF → atomicSetV1Ref`, uses the same mechanism. `gitrepo/ref_cas.go` owns a native `git update-ref --stdin` transaction: start, request `no-deref`, supply the new and expected old object IDs, prepare, inspect the reference while Git holds the prepared transaction's lock, then commit or abort. Input ref names are validated before entering the line-oriented protocol. A missing expected ref uses an all-zero ID of the correct hash width, covering SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories.

**The key design decision is different retry policies for different operations.** Ordinary persistent writes can hold Entire's per-ref flock, reread the tip, rebuild their tree, and retry. OPF's `CASPersistentRef` keeps its original expected hash fixed and **does not acquire that Entire flock**. It retries temporary native Git lock contention, with a bounded 16-attempt policy and jitter, but a real tip conflict aborts publication. A later checkpoint has not necessarily passed the filtering operation that produced A′. This distinction is more useful to explain than the PR title's word “serialize.”

**Errors and interruption.** `ErrRefCASConflict`, `ErrRefLocked`, and `ErrRefSymbolic` are separate contracts. A reference lookup failure is not automatically “absent”: a directory occupying a loose-ref path, permissions, or a namespace problem must retain its real diagnosis. Symbolic refs are rejected rather than followed or silently replaced. Transaction cancellation closes input so Git can abort, and a three-second `WaitDelay` bounds process cleanup. If Git acknowledged the commit, cancellation during subsequent waiting must not turn a successful publication into a reported failure. `V1RefMovedError` is used only when a definite conflict and a subsequent successful observation justify that diagnosis.

**Architecture and concepts.** This moves ref publication into `gitrepo`, with checkpoint and strategy callers retaining their own retry/recovery policy. Understand compare-and-swap, the linearization point, advisory versus native Git locks, immutable Git objects versus mutable refs, symbolic references, subprocess protocols, error identity, and ambiguous completion after cancellation. Publishing separate queued checkpoint refs remains separate operations; this PR is not an all-checkpoints atomic batch.

**Engineer questions.** Why can't OPF retry against B the way an ordinary writer does? Why is a lock necessary even with a hash comparison? At what moment can a symbolic reference be classified safely? What should a caller report if cancellation arrives just after `commit: ok`?

**Remember and verification evidence.** The test code exercises actual Git repositories, including files and reftable storage, concurrent changes, symbolic refs, cancellation and lock release, error classification, and OPF paths. The later #2304 refines error wrapping; #2310 fixes an inherited-environment hole in the shared command helper. Do not retroactively claim those later open changes were part of this merged PR.

{{sources:2211}}

{{pr:2038}}

**Problem and previous architecture.** Session end could persist a checkpoint, crash before saving the corresponding session-state progress, and then generate another checkpoint ID on retry. The same transcript window appeared twice. The underlying issue was two durable systems—checkpoint storage and local session bookkeeping—without one atomic commit spanning both.

**What you changed.** Session state now carries a `CondensationAttempt` with a reserved `CheckpointID` and `RecoveryPending` flag, supported by methods including `PendingCondensationID`, `BeginCondensationAttempt`, and the recovery/clear helpers. The normal end path goes through `markSessionEnded → MutateSessionState → PrepareSessionEndCondensation`, reserving the identifier while it already owns the session-state mutation. `CondenseAndMarkFullyCondensed` reuses that reservation, prepares eager condensation, persists the window, and only then resets the completed window and clears its attempt.

For example: reserve **C**, save that intent, write checkpoint C, then crash. The retry still names C. It does not make a new D just because the final bookkeeping was interrupted. Sessions with file changes remain tied to the commit path; ended sessions with meaningful no-file content can be condensed eagerly. An empty window can be marked complete without inventing a checkpoint.

**Recovery is evidence-based.** Legacy/interrupted cases can search for a matching already-written checkpoint through `findInterruptedCondensation`. Matching checks the session, strategy, window offsets/counts and other metadata, and compares the actual comparable redacted transcript. Externalized images are reinjected for comparison. A malformed candidate does not prevent finding a later exact match, but unresolved read errors are not proof that no checkpoint exists. `doctor` can establish a recovery attempt for eligible old state.

**Storage routing is part of idempotency.** A reserved ID also preserves the backend chosen when it was created. `ReservedSession` distinguishes this from a fresh `Session` write in the checkpoint write-request union. The routing store writes to the ID's backend and, when known to exist, its read-preferred migrated copy. All sibling session writes in the condensation use the reserved request shape. Otherwise changing the configured primary between attempt and retry could hide the repaired data. At this merged revision, a failure to probe the read-preferred backend logs a warning and still writes the original backend; this is deliberately fail-soft. #2131 proposes a different, stricter policy.

**Crucial edges.** Recovery must not substitute a different checkpoint ID after a Git commit has already fixed its trailer. An unrelated ended no-file session must not donate its reserved ID to a live agent's commit. Adoption clears source-local condensation bookkeeping so a session moved into another worktree does not reuse the wrong target's progress.

**Architecture and concepts.** Understand durable intent, idempotency keys, crash windows, state machines, exact-match recovery, checkpoint windows, and routing across storage migration. This is a practical recovery protocol, not a global exactly-once transaction across every store.

**Engineer questions.** Enumerate crashes before reservation, after reservation, after the checkpoint write, and after state advancement. Why isn't finding the same session ID enough to declare the retry complete? Which identifier wins when the commit trailer and a recovery candidate disagree?

**Remember and credit.** This PR was collaborative. Stefan's commits include interrupted-write integration coverage, preserving the commit's checkpoint ID during recovery, and fail-soft reserved routing. Your authored commits establish and harden the reservation/recovery design, including avoiding redundant session-state locking. Discuss the final behavior confidently while naming that collaboration.

{{sources:2038}}

{{pr:2241}}

**Problem and previous architecture.** Packages separately discovered or inferred `.git`, `commondir`, and worktree IDs. Some spawned Git and cached successful results; some inferred layout from path strings. A linked worktree, submodule, separately located Git directory, arbitrary bare directory name, or damaged pointer file could make these implementations disagree. The disagreement affected where state and locks were stored, not merely a displayed pathname.

**What you changed.** `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata(worktreeRoot)` becomes the owner of this filesystem interpretation. It returns `WorktreeMetadata{GitDir, CommonDir, WorktreeID}` or an error. The input is an explicit root; the resolver does not choose the current worktree, read process repository overrides, spawn Git, cache results, or decide a caller's fallback policy.

The path is: inspect `<root>/.git`; accept a directory or parse a `gitdir:` pointer relative to the worktree root; resolve `commondir` relative to that Git directory; compare physical directory identities. If GitDir and CommonDir are the same directory, this is a primary checkout or an ordinary submodule with an empty worktree ID. Otherwise validate that the administrative directory is an immediate child of `CommonDir/worktrees`, then derive its ID. The structural relationship replaces assumptions about a directory literally being named `.git` or `.bare`.

**Non-obvious hardening.** Metadata pointer reads are bounded at 16 KiB, with an extra byte used to detect overflow; error rendering is bounded too. Path cleaning cannot silently convert a broken `missing/../real` path into a valid one or change what `symlink/..` means. `os.SameFile` and physical resolution protect these identity decisions while retaining sensible returned path spelling. This resolver is not a blanket ban on symlinks and does not replace rooted I/O confinement.

`OpenPath` only falls back to bare-repository opening when worktree metadata is genuinely absent. Malformed metadata is not permission to reinterpret the repository as bare. Explicit `core.bare=false` is rejected for the bare fallback, while a suitable bare layout with the setting absent remains supported. Specialized opening failures must retain their diagnosis rather than being silently downgraded.

**Enforcement and architectural fit.** The new metadata ownership guard analyzes Go code with AST/type information, including package-level aliases and constants, to prevent new competing traversal logic. It has an audited migration allowance for existing consumers and legitimate policy checks. This first split establishes the owner and constraints; it does not itself migrate the entire repository. #2254, #2285, #2305, and the remaining-consumers branch do that incrementally.

**Concepts and questions.** Know per-worktree versus common metadata, Git pointer-file relativity, physical versus lexical identity, a pure mechanism versus caller policy, error taxonomies, bounded parsing, and architecture tests. An engineer may ask: why can an ordinary submodule have a `.git` file yet no worktree ID? Why is `filepath.Clean` insufficient? Why is a success cache dangerous after repository damage? Why not use `git rev-parse` everywhere?

**Remember.** The meaningful claim is a consistent, fresh filesystem answer when the root is already known. CWD discovery and semantic Git operations may still invoke Git. The tests include malformed layouts, pointer bounds, alias/path cases, bare opening, and guard bypass attempts; this is not proof that every conceivable filesystem race is eliminated.

{{sources:2241}}

{{pr:2254}}

**Problem and before.** Checkpoint storage had its own common-directory resolver using Git subprocesses and a success cache. A successful answer could outlive a broken or changed layout; shadow refs, persistent refs, queue files, and redaction caches could resolve metadata inconsistently with the new owner.

**Code change and path.** This split deletes `checkpoint/git_common_dir.go` and introduces `repository_metadata.go`. `repositoryDirs(repo)` obtains the worktree root and calls `gitrepo.ResolveWorktreeMetadata`. Checkpoint code in `ephemeral.go`, `shadow_ref.go`, `persistent_ref_update.go`, `refs_store.go`, `pushqueue.go`, and `redact_cache.go` uses that result. It migrates metadata resolution while preserving the consumers' rooted filesystem and locking behavior.

**Design and fit.** Mandatory persistent state and queue operations propagate resolution failures. The redaction cache is optional: inability to locate it disables reuse instead of making the underlying operation depend on cache availability. Removing discovery subprocesses does not justify removing `context.WithoutCancel` from post-publication bookkeeping: queueing already-published work still needs to survive cancellation of the original operation.

**Concepts and questions.** Understand dependency inversion through a shared owner, stale-success caching, required state versus optional cache, and cancellation boundaries. Why should a damaged layout fail a queue write but merely disable a cache? Why is “we removed the subprocess” insufficient reason to simplify the context handling?

**Remember and tests.** Regression coverage exercises successful resolution followed by damage, later repair, common-directory sharing across worktrees, and shadow-ref failure paths. This is **split part 2**, not the whole consolidation. It shipped separately from the still-open session and strategy migrations.

{{sources:2254}}

{{pr:2052}}

**Problem and before.** In linked worktrees, the path where Entire installed a local Codex hook file could differ from the path Codex actually discovered. Setup could appear successful while hooks were inactive, and status/doctor could confuse a local installation with an effective installation. Treating the shared Git directory's parent as universally authoritative also fails for submodules and unusual layouts.

**The final implementation separates two questions.** `ResolveWorktreeHooksPath` identifies the hook file Entire may mutate in the current worktree. `ResolveHookDiscovery` identifies what Codex will actually discover and diagnoses its state. `WorktreeHooksPath` and `DiscoveredHooksPath` are distinct types; `HookDiscovery` carries the discovered path, state, diagnostic, and worktree context. The resolver validates linked-worktree relationships using Git metadata, worktree identity and registration information, with layout-specific fallbacks. It explicitly avoids treating a user-wide Codex configuration as repository-owned.

**Call paths.** Enable/configure/remove paths use the worktree-owned path and hook mutation routines. Status and doctor consume hook diagnostics, including local-versus-discovered state, project-layer presence, malformed or unavailable files, freshness of managed event definitions, and trust gaps. `codexHookIssueFromDiagnostics` translates these findings into CLI behavior. A linked checkout whose effective hooks are healthy in the primary checkout should not get an endless “repair this local file” warning; the `worktree_path_not_discovered` diagnostic can remain available to structured output without producing that misleading warning.

**Trust and safe inspection.** Hook reads are bounded at 1 MiB and check file type and identity through rooted access. JSON handling preserves unfamiliar user fields. Trust matching accounts for canonical path aliases and parses the grouped hook/handler identity from the right, so a colon inside a path does not corrupt the key. Discovering a hook is not equivalent to authorizing it; Entire must not synthesize a user's approval.

**The change narrowed substantially during review.** Earlier commits pursued shared configuration migration, repository-wide effects, and locks. The **merged result writes local hooks with `os.WriteFile`** and does not introduce atomic rename or a new local flock for those writes.
